title: Parameter-space coverage (design of experiments): did sampling cover the space?
summary: Before running an expensive set of simulations at chosen parameter values, check that the design covers the space. The plot shows the marginal distribution of each parameter on the diagonal and every pairwise projection below it.

media.alt: A lower-triangular matrix of panels for four parameters p1 to p4: flat blue histograms on the diagonal, teal scatter plots of 64 points with light gridlines in the lower triangle, and a note at the upper right describing a Sobol design with n = 64.
media.caption: Reference render of class F7.8 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Did sampling cover the space?
read_the_figure.axes: Each scatter panel: one parameter against another, both scaled to 0 to 1. Diagonal: histograms of the single parameter in 8 bins. The lower triangle shows each pair once; the upper triangle is empty.
look_at: Are the diagonal histograms flat (each parameter covered evenly)?
In the pair plots, are there empty regions or clusters of points?
Do the gridlines show whether each strip holds the same number of points?
Is the design size and the method stated?
as_drawn: A Sobol design of 64 points in 4 parameters, scaled to the unit interval; the note at the upper right says so and explains that flat diagonal bars mean even coverage.
All four marginal histograms are flat: each of the 8 bins holds exactly 8 points (checked numerically for a scrambled Sobol set of 64).
The six pair plots show points spread without obvious holes or lines, with thin gridlines at every eighth.
Only two-dimensional projections are shown, and the diagonal panels have their y axes hidden, so the counts are not labelled.
read_the_figure.proves: A flat marginal and evenly filled pair plots show that no single parameter and no pair of parameters is badly covered. They cannot show gaps that exist only in three or four dimensions.
if_wrong: Uneven bars on the diagonal: the design over-samples some range of that parameter.
Visible lines or clusters in a pair plot: the design is correlated in those parameters.
A hole in a pair plot: no run explores that combination, so the response there is unknown.
must_check: projection matrix: a design in more than two dimensions can only be inspected by its one- and two-dimensional views, so the full set of pairs must be shown.

terms.meaning: Choosing the parameter values at which to run an expensive simulation or experiment.
A deterministic low-discrepancy sequence that fills the unit cube evenly; with 2^m points each strip of width 2^-k holds equally many points.
The distribution of one parameter alone, ignoring the others.
The view of a high-dimensional design in two of its coordinates.
Having no large empty regions and no clusters.
The number of grid points needed to cover a space grows exponentially with the number of parameters.

remember: A full grid with m levels in d dimensions needs m^d runs: 5^4 = 625, 10^4 = 10000.
A Sobol design with n = 2^m points has equal counts in each of the 2^k strips of every one-dimensional margin.
Flat marginals do not guarantee good joint coverage.
Scale parameters to the unit interval and back to physical ranges (log if needed).

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: The matrix puts every parameter on both a row and a column. On the diagonal a histogram shows how one parameter is covered; below it each scatter panel shows one pair, with a dot per run. Light gridlines at eighths let the eye count points per strip. Using the same unit scale in all panels makes them comparable.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: if you can only afford 64 runs, where you put them decides what you can learn. You cannot draw four-dimensional space, but you can draw every pair of parameters and the shadow of each one alone. If every shadow is flat and every pair fills its square, the design is at least not obviously lopsided. Seeing the whole matrix in one figure is much faster than reading numbers.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: The projections can be good while the four-dimensional design has holes: for example a diagonal arrangement of points looks even in each pair if the design is built from lattices. Flat marginals say nothing about joint coverage. Sixty-four points in four dimensions are sparse anyway: a regular grid with five levels per parameter would need 625. Physical parameters on a log scale need the design in log space, not in the raw units.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A single number such as the discrepancy or the minimum pairwise distance (F8.4) summarises coverage, but not where the holes are. Parallel coordinates show the whole design as lines. For higher dimensions, a distance-to-nearest-design histogram over random test points shows the largest empty regions.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add the discrepancy and the minimum distance between points to the note, colour the dots by the run's response in the lower triangle, and compare with a purely random design of the same size placed in the upper triangle.

steps.title: The cost of a grid
steps.note: A space-filling design with 64 points covers each margin and pair evenly with a tiny fraction of the grid cost.

steps.title: Equal strips in a Sobol design
steps.note: Checked numerically for a scrambled 4-dimensional Sobol set of 64 points; a random set of the same size gives counts from 4 to 11.

steps.title: A coverage measure that needs no formula book
steps.note: For 64 points in four dimensions a Sobol design has d_min of about 0.16 and a random design about 0.09 (averages over 20 draws, scratch script). The plot itself does not print it.

worked.title: Reading the design matrix in the reference render
worked.problem: (1) How many runs fall in each bin of each marginal for the render's design? (2) How many runs would a five-level full grid need, and how does that compare? (3) What can the matrix not tell you about this design?

solution.text: (1) The design has 64 points and the histograms have 8 bins, and all bars are equal.

(2) A five-level grid in four parameters needs 5^4 = 625 runs, about ten times more than the 64 used, and gives only five distinct values per parameter, whereas the Sobol design gives 64 distinct values of each.
(3) It shows only one- and two-dimensional views; a hole in a three- or four-dimensional sub-box, or a clustering of the response, would not be visible.

worked.answer: 8 runs per bin; 625 runs for a five-level grid against 64 here; the matrix cannot show gaps that exist only in three or four dimensions.

evaluate.q: You have budget for 64 runs but the response is rough in one parameter. Do you keep the design?
evaluate.hint: Sequential refinement, adding points where needed.

checks.q: What does a flat diagonal histogram mean?
checks.answer: That the values of that parameter are spread evenly over its range, with no part over- or under-sampled.

checks.q: A grid of 7 levels in 5 parameters needs how many runs?
All pair plots look even but the design is poor. How can that be?
checks.answer: The pair projections hide structure in three or more dimensions, such as all points lying on a lattice of planes or a hole in a three-dimensional box; check a discrepancy measure and the minimum distance.
